title: I'll come the rest (Pesikta Rabbati 44)
hookLine: a far-off prince is told: come back as far as you can, and I'll come the rest
tomorrow: why are babies born with their fists closed?

cards: A map app shows the whole route at once: hours of driving, dozens of turns, a little line that never seems to end. Sometimes the size of the trip is enough to keep you on the couch.
The same happens with people, and with faith: the way back looks so long that the first step never happens. One question for today: what if the way back is too far?

teach.b: Pesikta Rabbati answers with a parable, on the prophet's call: return, O Israel. A king's son was very far from his father. His friends told him: go back to your father.
He said: I can't. It's too far.

So his father sent word: come back as far as you're able, and I will come to you the rest of the way. That, says the midrash, is what God says in Malachi: "Return unto Me, and I will return unto you." Notice two things.
The father doesn't pretend the distance is small. And he doesn't ask for the whole trip, only as far as you're able. Last week the voice at Sinai reached each person according to their strength.
Here the road home works the same way. Now a neighbor.

In Islam, a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reports from God, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, says in effect: if My servant draws near to Me a hand's span, I draw near an arm's length; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running.
Shared ground: the human step is small, and God's answering step is bigger. The honest difference: the midrash is about a son who has wandered and must turn back, teshuvah, return.
The hadith describes any servant drawing near, with no wandering assumed, and God more than matching each step.
Each says it in its own words, from its own sources.

how: Jews read Hosea 14, 'Return, O Israel', on Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and this parable of the far-off prince is a familiar way of teaching teshuvah, return.

games.q: what does “i'll come the rest” mean?
o: God meets a returning person more than halfway
a guide always walks the road ahead of you
God waits until a person returns all the way

games.q: the road back — tap the pairs.
p: come as far as you're able
return unto Me, and I will return
walking to God, and God comes running

s: in the parable, the father insists his son make the whole trip home
he asks only as far as the son is able, and comes the rest himself.
the midrash seals the parable with 'Return unto Me, and I will return unto you'
the hadith and the midrash make exactly the same point
the midrash is a son turning back; the hadith, any servant drawing near, met more than halfway.

games.q: your friend stopped going to youth group a year ago. she says going back would mean explaining the whole year. by the parable, what's a fair first move?
o: go to one event, as far as she can manage, and let them meet her there.
wait until she's ready to explain everything that happened that year.
let it go; once you've drifted that far, the way back is closed.
games.why: the king asks his son to come only as far as he's able, and walks the rest himself. the first step doesn't have to cover the distance.

practice: Close your eyes and picture the road back to something you've drifted from: a person, a practice, a place. Take one step along it in your mind, only as far as you can honestly go today, and stop there.
Then rest where you are, and leave the rest of the road open.

wordCard.voice: I'll come the rest: the king's promise in Pesikta Rabbati. Come back as far as you're able, and I will come to you the rest of the way.

orig.note: Hebrew: return to Me, and I will return to you (Malachi 3:7), the verse the parable explains.

carryVoice: Your line: I'll come the rest. In the parable, nobody asked the son to walk the whole road.

sources.ref: Pesikta Rabbati 44 (on Hosea 14:2: the king's son far away; 'return as far as you are able, and I will come to you the rest of the way'; Malachi 3:7)
